title: Our students are consuming ultra-processed friends.
author: Paul Matthews
summary: Paul Matthews borrows Michael Moss's idea of ultra-processed food to describe AI companions that students use in place of human friends. He cites research suggesting two to four students in an average classroom regularly use AI companions such as Character.AI, Snapchat My AI and Replika. Their ingredients label, he says, is affection, affirmation and availability, which are good things in a relationship, so the harm lies in dosage and in what is left out: accountability, disagreement, compromise, limitation and rebuke. He points to Jonathan Haidt's criticism and a University of North Carolina survey of over 2,300 middle schoolers that linked companionship use of AI to more loneliness and anxiety. The result, he argues, is relational malnutrition, with a lonely student drinking seawater to quench thirst. He closes with three actions for teachers: share stories of formative friction, invite students to talk, and raise the issue with parents, who ask about academic integrity but rarely about relational integrity.
points: The ultra-processed food analogy locates the harm in the diet as a whole: AI companions supply affection, affirmation and availability while omitting the friction that real relationships require.
Missing relational nutrients are accountability, disagreement, compromise, limitation and rebuke, which are the things that teach students how their words affect others.
Early survey data links heavier companionship use of AI with loneliness and anxiety among middle schoolers, so the tool may worsen the problem it appears to solve.
Teachers can respond by telling stories of frustrating but formative experiences, making themselves open to conversation, and bringing the topic to parents.
Schools put their attention on academic integrity around AI, and Matthews argues relational integrity deserves equal attention.
quotes: And I want to argue that while ultra-processed food is bad for the body, AI-fuelled ultra-processed friends are bad for the soul.
Recent research suggests that in the average classroom, there are 2-4 students who regularly engage with AI companions.

And the harm is not due to detrimental ingredients. There is nothing wrong with affection, affirmation, or availability. We are created for relationship, and these are the hallmarks of a good relationship. The harm comes from the dosage and the absence of other nutrients.

These elements are the natural companions of affection, affirmation, and availability in a good human relationship. They are valuable relational micronutrients without which the student becomes socially malnourished.
The study surveyed more than 2,300 middle schoolers and found that students who used AI more often for companionship were also more likely to report loneliness and anxiety.
A lonely student turning to an AI chatbot for companionship is like a thirsty student drinking a cup of seawater for hydration. The “solution” to the problem merely amplifies the problem.
I got lots of questions about academic integrity but very few about relational integrity. The brain is important, but so is the heart.
